title: How Fossils Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how fossils form and how paleontologists find and excavate them. They open with the recent University of Missouri find of Lucy's missing foot bones showing she walked upright. They cover trace fossils (footprints, tooth marks, coprolites, plaster-cast style molds), body fossils, and the process of permineralization in sedimentary rock, where organic material decays and minerals like calcium, iron and carbonate fill the pores. They discuss petrified wood, desiccation (dried remains such as the Smithsonian musk ox), frozen fossils such as the baby woolly mammoth Liuba, tar pits (La Brea), peat bog preservation (Tollund Man), and amber, including the Jurassic Park dino-DNA idea and why it is doubtful. They explain radiometric dating (carbon-14 limited to about 60,000 years; potassium-40 and uranium-238 for older rock), how to excavate carefully and call a museum, the fossil record's incompleteness, transitional fossils such as the baleen whale with teeth, punctuated equilibrium versus gradual evolution, and living fossils like the horseshoe crab, coelacanth and ginkgo. The episode ends with listener mail from Ali, a marimba competitor who was upset by a bronze medal.

segments.title: Intro and Lucy's foot bones
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the topic and the How Fossils Work article, then discuss how University of Missouri researchers used recently found foot bones to show that Lucy walked upright.

segments.title: Types of fossils: trace fossils and bone fossils
segments.summary: Chuck describes trace fossils such as footprints and tooth marks, and bone fossils, which are needed to reconstruct dinosaurs. They note that a fossil is organic material that has undergone fossilization, unlike ordinary buried bone.

segments.title: Sedimentary rock and the Earth's crust
segments.summary: The hosts explain that most fossils are in sedimentary rock in the crust, formed as suspended sediment settles and hardens. They note that plate movement and river erosion, such as the Colorado River in the Grand Canyon, can expose fossils.

segments.title: Decomposition, burial and permineralization
segments.summary: A creature buried quickly by sediment is protected from decomposers. Soft tissue breaks down while the inorganic mineral structure of bone remains. Minerals such as iron and carbonate fill the porous bone and turn it into rock in the bone's shape, which takes millions of years.

segments.title: Trace fossil casts and molds
segments.summary: Hosts compare animal footprints filled with sediment to plaster casts made as children. They say a footprint can be preserved as a mold, and plants can also leave impressions of the foot that made the track.

segments.title: Coprolites and the CIA's study of Gorbachev's feces
segments.summary: Chuck names fossilized poop, or coprolites, as a favorite trace fossil that reveals diet. He tells a story about the CIA analyzing Gorbachev's feces during a US visit in the 1980s to learn about his health.

segments.title: Petrified wood and desiccation
segments.summary: Petrified wood is described as wood turned to rock by the same process as bone. Desiccation in dry caves preserves remains by drying them out, which can keep skin and soft tissue, as with a prehistoric musk ox or cow displayed at the Smithsonian.

segments.title: Frozen fossils, Liuba, and tar pits
segments.summary: Animals trapped in ice are preserved, including hair. Liuba, a baby woolly mammoth found in Siberia after about forty years in permafrost, is described. The hosts also discuss La Brea tar pits in Los Angeles and a small active tar puddle Chuck saw while filming.

segments.title: Peat bogs, Tollund Man, and amber
segments.summary: Peat bogs preserve bodies, as with Tollund Man, a sacrificed man from Denmark wearing a cap, found in the 1950s. Amber is discussed as a preservation medium, and the hosts examine the Jurassic Park idea of extracting dinosaur DNA from mosquitoes in amber, which a researcher later debunked as not feasible.

segments.title: Rarity of fossils, dating, and excavation
segments.summary: Fossils are rare because a rare combination of chance is needed to form one. Paleontologists locate fossils by dating rock layers with radiometric methods such as carbon-14 (limited to about 60,000 years), and potassium-40 and uranium-238 for older rock. The hosts advise calling a museum and explain careful excavation, including plaster jacketing and using the plane of weakness.

segments.title: Fossil record, transitional fossils and evolution
segments.summary: The fossil record shows past life but is incomplete. Transitional fossils, such as a 25-million-year-old baleen whale with sharp teeth, show intermediate forms. Stephen J. Gould's punctuated equilibrium is described as an explanation for gaps, versus gradual evolution, and the hosts say it is a hypothesis.

segments.title: Living fossils
segments.summary: Living fossils are organisms that look like ancient fossils, such as the horseshoe crab, ginkgo, and the coelacanth, which was thought extinct until found off South America.

segments.title: Listener mail: Ali and the bronze medal
segments.summary: Ali, a marimba competitor from Indiana who won a bronze medal, wrote in saying the hosts' comments about bronze medals made her cry. The hosts respond with encouragement.
